title: Christianity: key beliefs
summary: What Christians believe about God — one God, all-powerful, all-loving and just, known as the Trinity — how the world was created, and what happens after death. The problem of evil sits in here and is a favourite 12-mark question.

blocks.text: Christianity is monotheistic: Christians believe in one God. The Nicene Creed opens "We believe in one God", and the first of the Ten Commandments says "You shall have no other gods before me" (Exodus 20:3). There are three main branches — Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant — and all share this belief.

rows: Omnipotent
All-powerful — nothing God cannot do
"Nothing is impossible with God" (Luke 1:37). God created the universe ex nihilo — from nothing.
Omnibenevolent (loving)
All-loving
"For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son" (John 3:16). "God is love" (1 John 4:8).
Just
Fair — brings about what is right
"All his ways are just" (Deuteronomy 32:4).

blocks.text: Why it matters today: because God is loving, Christians try to love others — "Love is patient, love is kind" (1 Corinthians 13:4). Because God is just, Christians work for fairness and expect to be judged. Because God is omnipotent, they pray, trusting God can act.

sections.title: The problem of evil and suffering

blocks.text: If God is all-loving, God would want to end suffering. If God is all-powerful, God could end it. Yet suffering exists. This clash is called the inconsistent triad (from the Greek philosopher Epicurus). A religious answer to it is called a theodicy.

items: Free will (Augustine; Alvin Plantinga) — God gave humans free will so their love could be real. Most suffering comes from people misusing it.
Original sin (Augustine) — evil entered the world when Adam and Eve disobeyed God; everyone is born with a tendency to sin.
Vale of soul-making (John Hick) — suffering gives us the chance to grow, show compassion and become better people.
Jesus suffered too — God is not distant from suffering but shared it on the cross.

sections.title: The oneness of God and the Trinity

blocks.text: Christians believe in one God in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. It is not three Gods. Three statements hold at once: there is only one God; each person is fully God; the persons are not the same as each other.

items: God the Father — creator of all, "Our Father in heaven" (the Lord's Prayer).
God the Son — Jesus, fully God and fully human.
God the Holy Spirit — the unseen power of God at work in the world, guiding and sustaining believers.

blocks.title: Evidence for the Trinity
blocks.text: At Jesus' baptism all three appear together: the Son is baptised, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and the Father's voice says "You are my Son, whom I love" (Mark 1:11).

"In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth… and the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters. And God said, 'Let there be light'" (Genesis 1:1-3). This teaches that God created everything, that creation was good, and that the Spirit was present.
"In the beginning was the Word… Through him all things were made" (John 1:1-3). "The Word" means Jesus, God the Son. So all three persons of the Trinity were involved in creation.

headers: Non-literal (most Christians, including the Catholic Church)
rows: Genesis is an exact account: six days, a young earth.
Genesis carries religious truth — God made the world and it is good — not a scientific account. It fits with the Big Bang and evolution.

sections.title: The afterlife: resurrection, judgement, heaven and hell

blocks.text: Most Christians believe death is not the end. The Apostles' Creed says Jesus "will come to judge the living and the dead" and affirms "the resurrection of the body, and the life everlasting".

items: Resurrection — some believe in a physical, transformed body (the Catholic view); others in a spiritual resurrection. "It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:44).
Judgement — in the Parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25) people are judged on how they treated those in need: feeding the hungry, welcoming strangers, visiting prisoners.
Heaven — eternal happiness with God. "My Father's house has many rooms" (John 14:2). Some see it as a place, others as a state.
Hell — traditionally "eternal fire" (Matthew 25:41); many modern Christians see it as being cut off from God for ever.
Purgatory — Catholics believe in a state of cleansing before heaven.
Universalism — some believe a loving God will in the end save everyone.

blocks.text: Why it matters: belief in judgement encourages Christians to live well and help others now; belief in heaven gives comfort when someone dies.

keyTerms.definition: Belief in one God.
All-powerful.
All-loving.
All-knowing.
Present everywhere.
Fair; bringing about what is right.
A religious response to the problem of evil and suffering.
One God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
Term at the start of John's gospel for God the Son, Jesus.
Out of nothing — how God created the universe.
When God will judge every soul and reward or punish it.

examTips: Name the source: "the Apostles' Creed says…", "in John 3:16…". A named teaching is worth the extra mark on a 5-marker.
For the problem of evil, say what the problem is before giving the theodicies.
commonMistakes: Saying Christians believe in three Gods. One God, three persons.
Treating all Christians as creationists. Most read Genesis non-literally.

resources.title: AQA GCSE Religious Studies A — specification and past papers
resources.description: The official spec, specimen papers and mark schemes. The mark schemes show exactly what a 12-mark answer needs.

title: Christianity: Jesus Christ and salvation
summary: Who Jesus is (God incarnate), what happened at the crucifixion, resurrection and ascension, and why it matters: sin separates people from God, and Jesus' death and resurrection make salvation possible.

blocks.text: Incarnation means "becoming flesh". Christians believe God became a human being in Jesus — fully God and fully human. "The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us" (John 1:14). Matthew and Luke describe the virgin birth: Mary conceived through the Holy Spirit. It is celebrated at Christmas.

Jesus is called the Son of God. At his trial, asked if he was "the Son of the Blessed One", he replied "I am" (Mark 14:62) — and was accused of blasphemy. Believing he was God incarnate helps Christians explain his miracles and resurrection.

steps.title: Crucifixion (Good Friday)
steps.text: Jesus was executed on a cross. Being fully human, he felt real pain. He forgave those who crucified him — "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34) — and his last words were "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit" (Luke 23:46). A Roman centurion said "Surely this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39).

steps.title: Resurrection (Easter Sunday)
steps.text: Women including Mary Magdalene found the tomb empty. Over 40 days Jesus appeared to many, including "doubting" Thomas, who touched his wounds.

steps.title: Ascension
steps.text: Forty days after the resurrection Jesus returned to the Father: "he left them and was taken up into heaven" (Luke 24:51). Before leaving he gave the Great Commission — go and make disciples.

blocks.title: Why the resurrection matters
blocks.text: "If Christ has not been raised, our preaching is useless and so is your faith" (1 Corinthians 15:14). It shows Jesus defeated death and promises believers eternal life.

Sin is any thought or action that separates people from God or goes against God's law. Original sin is the belief that humans are born with a tendency to sin, inherited from Adam and Eve's disobedience in the Garden of Eden (Genesis 3). Most Christians read the story non-literally, as a truth about human nature and temptation. God gave free will, so people can choose good or evil.
"All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23).
Salvation means being saved from sin and its consequences and brought back to God, with eternal life in heaven.

rows: Law / good works
Faith shown by obeying God's law and doing good — e.g. the Ten Commandments, helping the poor.
"Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead" (James 2:17).
Grace
Salvation is a free gift of God's love, given through faith in Jesus. It cannot be earned.
"It is by grace you have been saved, through faith… not by works" (Ephesians 2:8-9).
Spirit
The Holy Spirit works in believers, guiding them to live a holy life and strengthening their faith.
The Spirit given at Pentecost and through baptism.

blocks.text: Many Christians combine them: salvation is a gift of grace, and good works are the response to it. Catholics stress faith and works together; many Protestants stress grace through faith alone.

sections.title: The role of Christ in salvation: atonement

blocks.text: Atonement means restoring the relationship between people and God — "at-one-ment". Christians believe Jesus' death paid the price for human sin and his resurrection defeated death. "He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2).

blocks.caption: The Jesus bridge. Sin leaves a gap between people and a holy God; the cross bridges it.

blocks.text: Christians remember this in the Eucharist (Holy Communion), sharing bread and wine as Jesus did at the Last Supper. "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6).

keyTerms.definition: Becoming flesh — God becoming human in Jesus.
Jesus' execution on a cross on Good Friday.
Rising from the dead — Jesus on Easter Sunday.
Jesus returning to the Father in heaven, 40 days after the resurrection.
Any thought or action that separates humans from God.
The inbuilt tendency to do wrong, inherited from Adam and Eve.
Being saved from sin and its consequences, and admitted to heaven.
God's love, freely given — it does not need to be earned.
Restoring the relationship between people and God through Jesus' death and resurrection.
A religious offence, including claiming to be God.

examTips: Learn "at-one-ment" — it lets you define atonement in five words.
For "Without Jesus' death and resurrection there would be no salvation", use grace and atonement FOR, and law / good works AGAINST.
commonMistakes: Mixing up resurrection (rising from the dead) and ascension (going up to heaven 40 days later).
Writing "Jesus was half God and half human". Fully God AND fully human.

resources.title: BBC Bitesize — GCSE Religious Studies
resources.description: Subject root. Pick AQA, then the Christianity, Islam and themes sections.

title: Islam: key beliefs
summary: The core beliefs of Islam: Tawhid (one God), God's nature, angels, predestination and life after death — and how Sunni and Shi'a Muslims set them out differently in the six articles of faith and the five roots of Usul ad-Din.

sections.title: Six articles of faith and five roots of Usul ad-Din

blocks.text: After Muhammad died there was a dispute about who should lead the Muslims, which produced two main groups. Sunni Muslims are the large majority worldwide; Shi'a Muslims are the minority. They share most beliefs but list them differently.

rows: Tawhid — the oneness of God
Tawhid — the oneness of God
Angels
Adalat — the justice of God
Holy books
Nubuwwah — prophethood
Prophethood (Risalah)
Imamah — the imamate
Day of Judgement (Akhirah)
Mi'ad — the Day of Judgement and resurrection
Supremacy of God's will (predestination)

blocks.title: Similarities and differences
blocks.text: Both start with Tawhid, and both include prophets and the Day of Judgement. Only Sunni lists angels, holy books and predestination as separate articles (Shi'a Muslims still believe in them). Only Shi'a lists God's justice and the imamate.

Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam: God is one, unique and indivisible. "Say, He is God the One, God the eternal. He begot no one nor was He begotten. No one is comparable to Him" (Qur'an 112). Muslims say it daily in the Shahadah: "There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah."
Shirk — treating anything as equal to God — is the worst sin. That is why there are no pictures or statues of God or of the Prophet in a mosque.

rows: Omnipotent
All-powerful. "He is in charge of all things" (Qur'an 6:102).
Beneficent
All-loving and generous — seen in the gift of life and the world.
Merciful
Forgives those who are truly sorry. Every surah but one opens "In the name of God, the Lord of Mercy, the Giver of Mercy".
Fair and just (Adalat)
Treats everyone fairly and judges actions — rewarding good and punishing evil.
Immanent
Close to and involved with creation.
Transcendent
Beyond and outside creation, not limited by it.

blocks.text: Muslims know God through the 99 names, such as "The Merciful" and "The Just".

Angels are spiritual beings made from light. They have no free will and always obey God. They bring God's messages to the prophets and watch over people: "Each person has angels before him and behind, watching over him by God's command" (Qur'an 13:11).

items: Jibril (Gabriel) — brought the Qur'an to Muhammad, starting on the Night of Power on Mount Hira when Muhammad was 40.
Mika'il (Michael) — angel of mercy; rewards the righteous and sends rain to nourish the earth.
Israfil — will blow the trumpet to announce the Day of Judgement.
Izra'il — the angel of death.
Two recording angels note every person's good and bad deeds.

blocks.text: Predestination (al-Qadr) is the idea that God knows or decides everything that will happen. "Only what God has decreed will happen to us" (Qur'an 9:51).

rows: God has already decided everything; it is written in the Book of Decrees. Yet humans are still responsible for their choices.
God KNOWS everything that will happen but does not DECIDE it. Humans have free will. (A parent knows which bowl a toddler will pick, but the child still chooses.)

blocks.text: Link to judgement: if people had no free will, judging them would be unfair. Both groups hold that people are accountable on the Day of Judgement.

steps.title: Death and barzakh
steps.text: The soul enters barzakh ("barrier"), a state of waiting. Two angels question the dead about their faith. No one can cross back to put things right.

steps.title: Day of Judgement
steps.text: Israfil blows the trumpet, the world ends, and everyone is resurrected and judged on their deeds and faith. "Whoever has done an atom's weight of good will see it" (Qur'an 99:7).

steps.title: Jannah or Jahannam
steps.text: Jannah (paradise) is a garden of joy, "a reward for what they used to do" (Qur'an 56:24). Jahannam (hell) is fire and torment for those who reject God or do evil (Qur'an 56:42).

blocks.text: Why it matters: knowing they are accountable, Muslims try to follow God's will, pray, and help others.

keyTerms.definition: The oneness and unity of God.
Associating anything with God — the gravest sin.
The Arabic name for God.
The justice of God — one of the Shi'a five roots.
God is close to and involved in the world.
God is beyond and outside the world.
Spiritual beings made from light, who act as God's messengers.
The idea that God knows or decides everything that will happen.
Everlasting life after death.
The state of waiting between death and the Day of Judgement.
Paradise / hell.

examTips: The 1-mark MCQ often asks which is NOT an article of faith. The imamate is Shi'a, not one of the six Sunni articles.
For a 4-mark "Explain two ways belief in … influences Muslims today", say what the belief is, then what Muslims DO because of it.
commonMistakes: Muddling the two lists. Angels and holy books are Sunni articles; justice and the imamate are Shi'a roots.
Getting Jibril and Mika'il the wrong way round. Jibril brought the Qur'an.

resources.title: BBC Bitesize — GCSE Religious Studies
resources.description: Subject root. Pick AQA, then the Christianity, Islam and themes sections.

title: Islam: authority
summary: Where Muslims get their authority from: the prophets (Risalah) — especially Adam, Ibrahim and Muhammad — the holy books, above all the Qur'an, and for Shi'a Muslims the imams.

blocks.text: Risalah is the communication between God and humans through prophets. Many Muslims believe there have been about 124,000 prophets; 25 are named in the Qur'an. "Every community is sent a messenger" (Qur'an 10:47). They include Adam, Ibrahim (Abraham), Musa (Moses), Dawud (David), Isa (Jesus) and Muhammad.

rows: Adam
First man and first prophet. Made by God from clay (Qur'an 32:7). With Hawwa (Eve) he lived in the Garden, was tempted by Iblis and ate from the forbidden tree, but repented and was forgiven.
Ibrahim

Rejected idol worship and taught there is one God. Willing to sacrifice his son when God asked — remembered at Id-ul-Adha. Rebuilt the Ka'aba with his son Isma'il; remembered on Hajj. "God took Abraham as a friend" (Qur'an 4:125).
Muhammad
The final prophet, the "Seal of the Prophets" (Qur'an 33:40). Received the Qur'an through Jibril. The perfect example of how to live.

steps.title: c. 570 CE
steps.text: Born in Makkah into the Quraysh tribe. Orphaned and raised by his uncle Abu Talib. Married Khadijah.

steps.title: 610 CE
steps.text: Night of Power: aged 40, Jibril revealed the first words of the Qur'an on Mount Hira.

steps.title: 622 CE
steps.text: Hijrah — persecuted in Makkah, he moved to Madinah.

steps.title: 630 CE
steps.text: Returned to Makkah, removed the idols from the Ka'aba.

rows: Qur'an
Muhammad, through Jibril, over about 23 years
Tawrat (Torah)
Musa (Moses)
Zabur (Psalms)
Dawud (David)
Injil (Gospel)
Isa (Jesus)
Sahifah (Scrolls of Abraham)
Ibrahim — now lost

blocks.text: The Qur'an is the final, complete and unchanged word of God, and the highest authority. "This is the Scripture in which there is no doubt, containing guidance for those who are mindful of God" (Qur'an 2:2). It is recited in Arabic; someone who knows it by heart is a hafiz. The earlier books were from God, but Muslims believe their texts were lost or changed over time, so they do not carry the same authority.
When Muhammad died, Sunni Muslims accepted Abu Bakr, his father-in-law and close friend, as the first caliph (leader), followed by Umar, Uthman and then Ali.

Shi'a Muslims believe Muhammad chose Ali — his cousin and son-in-law — to succeed him, and that leadership should stay in the Prophet's family. They follow twelve imams: Ali and his descendants through Fatimah, Muhammad's daughter. Imams are chosen by God, are infallible (cannot make mistakes) and guard the true meaning of the Qur'an. Most Shi'a believe the twelfth imam is hidden and will return.

blocks.title: The knowledge organiser gets this backwards
blocks.text: The school sheet says the imams had no family connection to Muhammad. They did — they were his descendants through Ali and Fatimah, and that family link is exactly why Shi'a Muslims follow them. Write it this way in the exam.

keyTerms.definition: Prophethood — communication between God and humans through prophets.
A person who proclaims the message of God.
Muhammad — the final prophet; there will be none after him.
Spiritual being made from fire, thrown out of paradise for refusing to bow to Adam (Shaytan).
The cube-shaped building in Makkah — the holiest place in Islam.
The holy book revealed to Muhammad by Jibril; God's final revelation.
Successor to Muhammad as leader of the Sunni community.
1. Leader of communal prayer. 2. In Shi'a Islam, Ali and his descendants who led the community.
The divine appointment of the imams.

examTips: For the 12-marker "Holy books are not important for Muslims today", FOR is hard to argue — say some Muslims rely more on hadith, scholars or imams, and the earlier books are lost or changed. AGAINST: the Qur'an is God's unchanged word, guides daily life and law (Shari'ah).
commonMistakes: Saying Muhammad wrote the Qur'an. It was revealed to him; Muslims believe it is God's word.

resources.title: BBC Bitesize — GCSE Religious Studies
resources.description: Subject root. Pick AQA, then the Christianity, Islam and themes sections.

title: Theme A: Sex, marriage and divorce
summary: Christian and Muslim teaching on sexuality, sex before and outside marriage, contraception, marriage, same-sex marriage, cohabitation and divorce — set against how British law and society see them.

blocks.text: British attitudes have changed a lot: contraception and legal abortion reduced the risk of pregnancy, and same-sex marriage became legal in England and Wales in 2014. The age of consent is 16.

rows: Heterosexual relationships are part of God's plan — man and woman become "one flesh" (Genesis 2:24) and "increase in number". Views on homosexuality differ. The Catholic Church says homosexual orientation is not sinful but sexual acts are. Some quote Leviticus 18:22. Liberal Christians accept same-sex relationships as loving and equal; Quakers and Methodists will marry same-sex couples.

The only permitted sexual relationship is between husband and wife — a gift from God. Most Muslims believe the Qur'an and hadith teach that homosexual acts are against God's will, citing the story of Lut (Qur'an 7:80-81). Some liberal Muslims accept same-sex relationships.

blocks.text: Sex before marriage is now widely accepted in Britain. Adultery (sex outside marriage) is still widely seen as wrong because it involves lies and betrayal of trust, and can hurt children.

rows: Most Christians believe sex belongs in marriage. Catholic teaching: every sexual act must be within marriage. Some liberal Christians accept sex before marriage in a loving, committed relationship. Almost all say adultery is wrong — it breaks the wedding vows and the commandment "You shall not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:14).

Sex before marriage and adultery are both zina — forbidden. "Do not go anywhere near adultery: it is an outrage and an evil path" (Qur'an 17:32). Muslims avoid situations that could lead to it, e.g. a man and a woman who are not related being alone together.

blocks.text: Artificial contraception (the pill, condoms) is widely accepted in Britain. Natural family planning means only having sex at times in the woman's cycle when she is less likely to conceive.

rows: Catholic Church: sex has two purposes — making new life and expressing love — which must not be separated, so only natural methods are allowed. Church of England and most Protestants: artificial contraception is fine for responsible family planning, though some object to methods like the morning-after pill, which they see as like abortion.

No direct teaching in the Qur'an, so opinion is divided. Most Muslims accept contraception within marriage to space children or protect the mother's health, but not to avoid having children altogether. Some quote "Do not kill your children for fear of poverty" (Qur'an 17:31) against it; others "God wishes to lighten your burden" (Qur'an 4:28) in favour.

sections.title: The nature and purpose of marriage

blocks.text: Marriage is a legal union that gives security, legal rights and a public lifelong commitment. Civil partnerships for same-sex couples came in 2004.

rows: A gift from God at creation. Its purposes: lifelong companionship and support, a loving sexual relationship, having children ("be fruitful and increase in number", Genesis 1:28) and bringing them up in the faith. For Catholics it is a sacrament.

The foundation of family life and society. "There is no institution in Islam more beloved to God than marriage" (hadith). A man who marries completes half his religion (hadith). Marriage (nikah) is a contract; love grows within it. Some marriages are arranged, with both partners' consent.

blocks.text: Cohabitation is a couple living together without being married. It is common in Britain, often before marriage.

rows: Same-sex marriage: the Catholic Church and Church of England do not marry same-sex couples, as they see marriage as one man and one woman; many opposed the law because it changed what marriage is, not because they oppose equal rights. Quakers and Methodists do. Cohabitation: Catholics see it as wrong; many Protestants accept it if the couple are committed, often as a step to marriage.
Same-sex marriage is not accepted, as homosexual acts are forbidden. Cohabitation is not allowed — sex outside marriage is zina.

blocks.text: Reasons for divorce include adultery, abuse, money problems and simply growing apart. Since 2022 a couple in England and Wales can divorce without blaming either partner ("no-fault" divorce).

rows: Jesus: "Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her" (Mark 10:11). Matthew 19:9 allows an exception for unfaithfulness. Catholic Church: marriage is a permanent sacrament, so no divorce; an annulment may declare a marriage was never valid. Church of England: divorce is allowed and remarriage in church is at the vicar's discretion. Many see divorce as the lesser of two evils.

Allowed as a last resort, but "of all lawful things, divorce is the most hated by God" (hadith). Both men and women have the right to divorce; Muhammad married a divorced woman. A man declares talaq; then a three-month waiting period (iddah) gives time to reconcile and check whether the wife is pregnant. A woman can seek a divorce through a court (khul').
Sanctity of marriage vows
Vows made before God ("till death us do part") are sacred and should not be broken. "What God has joined together, let no one separate" (Mark 10:9). Argues against divorce.
Compassion
Jesus showed compassion and forgiveness. Forcing someone to stay in an abusive or loveless marriage causes harm, especially to children. Argues that divorce can be the right thing.

keyTerms.definition: Sexually attracted to people of the opposite sex.
Sexually attracted to people of the same sex.
Sex between a married person and someone who is not their spouse.
Sexual activity outside marriage — forbidden in Islam.
Methods used to prevent pregnancy.
Using contraception to control how many children a couple have and when.
A couple living together without being married.
A ceremony that gives God's grace; for Catholics, marriage is one.
A Catholic ruling that a marriage was never valid.
Divorce declared by a Muslim husband.
The three-month waiting period before a Muslim divorce is final.

examTips: "Contrasting" means different views — e.g. Catholic vs Church of England on contraception, or Christianity vs Islam.
"Similar" means two views that agree — e.g. Christianity and Islam both teach adultery is wrong.
Cohabitation is a likely 4-marker: Catholic (wrong) vs many Anglicans (acceptable if committed) is the cleanest contrast.
commonMistakes: Saying "all Christians" believe X. Name the group — Catholic, Church of England, liberal.

resources.title: BBC Bitesize — GCSE Religious Studies
resources.description: Subject root. Pick AQA, then the Christianity, Islam and themes sections.

title: Theme A: Families and gender equality
summary: Types of family, what families are for, same-sex parents and polygamy, the roles of men and women, and religious teaching on gender equality, prejudice and discrimination.

rows: Nuclear
A couple and their children — still the most common in the West.
Extended
Includes grandparents and other relatives, often living together or close by.
Single-parent
One parent bringing up children.
Step (blended)
Formed when a parent remarries someone with children of their own.
Same-sex parents
Two parents of the same sex.

Love is at the heart of family life — a family is where a child learns to love. Parents should provide for their family: anyone who does not "has denied the faith" (1 Timothy 5:8). Children should "honour your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12).

The extended family is the basis of Islamic society. Elderly parents are cared for with kindness: "Your Lord has commanded that you should worship none but Him, and be kind to your parents" (Qur'an 17:23).

items: Procreation — having children. "Be fruitful and increase in number" (Genesis 1:28).
Stability — a secure base that keeps society stable.
Protection of children — meeting their physical and emotional needs.
Educating children in a faith — Christian parents promise at baptism to bring their children up as Christians; Muslim parents teach the Qur'an and take children to the mosque.

blocks.text: Islam: "For every tree there is a fruit, and the fruit of the heart is the child" (hadith). The Qur'an describes married people as "guarded", their family a fortress protecting them from sin and loneliness.

rows: Same-sex parents
Catholic Church and some others say a child needs a mother and a father as role models. Liberal Christians say a loving home matters most.
Most Muslims do not accept it, as homosexual relationships are forbidden.
Polygamy (illegal in the UK)
Some figures in the Old Testament had several wives, but Christians teach marriage is one man and one woman.
A man may have up to four wives, but only if he can treat them equally: "if you fear you cannot be equitable, then marry only one" (Qur'an 4:3). Muslims in the UK follow UK law.

sections.title: Roles of men and women, gender equality and discrimination

blocks.text: Gender equality means men and women have the same rights and opportunities. Gender prejudice is unfairly judging someone because of their gender; discrimination is acting on that prejudice. The Sex Discrimination Act 1975 made discrimination illegal, but a gender pay gap remains.

rows: All are created equal in God's image: "There is neither… male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). Jesus treated women with respect, e.g. Mary Magdalene. Traditional view: the man is head of the family, from a literal reading of texts like Ephesians 5:22. The Church of England has had women priests since 1994 and women bishops since 2014 — Paul sent Phoebe as a church representative. The Catholic Church allows only men to be priests, because Jesus' apostles were men.

Men and women were created from a single soul and are spiritually equal, with equal rewards (Qur'an 33:35). "We created you all from a single man and a single woman" (Qur'an 49:13). Traditionally men provide for the family and women raise the children, and the mother's role is highly honoured; in many British Muslim families both parents work. Muslims say discrimination against women in some countries comes from culture, not the Qur'an.

keyTerms.definition: A couple and their children.
A family that includes grandparents and other relatives.
A family formed when a parent remarries.
Bringing babies into the world.
Having more than one wife or husband at the same time.
Men and women having the same rights and opportunities.
Unfairly judging someone because of their gender.
Acting against someone because of their gender.

examTips: For "Give one religious teaching about gender discrimination", Galatians 3:28 is the safest one-liner.
commonMistakes: Confusing prejudice (a thought or attitude) with discrimination (an action).

title: Theme B: Religion, violence, terrorism and war
summary: Peace, justice, forgiveness and reconciliation; violent protest and terrorism; why wars are fought; and the three big religious positions on war — just war, holy war and pacifism.

rows: Peace — absence of conflict; harmony
"Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9). Quakers are pacifists.
Islam comes from the same root as salam, peace. Muslims greet each other "as-salamu alaikum" — peace be with you.
Justice — what is right and fair
Many wars are fought to bring justice, at the cost of peace while they last.
"The Just" is one of the 99 names of God. Injustice should not be ignored.
Forgiveness — letting go of blame
Forgive "seventy times seven" (Matthew 18:22). God forgives all who ask in faith.
God is merciful, so Muslims should forgive: "anyone who forgives and puts things right will have his reward from God" (Qur'an 42:40).
Reconciliation — restoring friendly relations
The Community of the Cross of Nails, based at Coventry Cathedral, works for reconciliation worldwide.
"When aggressive people address them, they reply with words of peace" (Qur'an 25:63).

blocks.title: Organiser slip
blocks.text: The school sheet says Canterbury Cathedral. The Cross of Nails comes from Coventry Cathedral, bombed in 1940.

Protest is a democratic right in the UK; police must be told six days before a march and can ban one likely to turn violent. Terrorism is the unlawful use of violence, usually against civilians, to achieve a political goal — for example the Manchester Arena bombing on 22 May 2017, which killed 22 people.

rows: Jesus taught "turn the other cheek" (Matthew 5:39). Most Christians support peaceful protest, like Martin Luther King Jr in the US civil rights movement. A few argue for "righteous anger" because Jesus overturned the tables in the Temple. Terrorism is wrong: innocent people are the victims and it fails the just war criteria. Paul taught Christians to obey the authorities (Romans 13:1).

Fighting is allowed only in self-defence and only against those who fight you. Most Muslims support peaceful protest only. Terrorism is wrong: "Do not take life, which God has made sacred" (Qur'an 17:33). "Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had killed all mankind" (Qur'an 5:32). It fails the conditions for lesser jihad.
Greed — selfish desire for land, resources or power
"The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil" (1 Timothy 6:10).
God does not like those who are miserly and boastful (Qur'an 4:36-37).
Self-defence — protecting yourself or others
Most Christians accept it — e.g. Britain in the Second World War.
"Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms because they have been wronged" (Qur'an 22:39).
Retaliation — hitting back after being harmed
"Eye for eye" (Exodus 21:24), but Jesus replaced it: "turn the other cheek" (Matthew 5:38-39).
"Fair retribution saves life for you" (Qur'an 2:179), but forgiveness is the better response.

blocks.title: Organiser slip
blocks.text: The sheet quotes "money is the root of all evil". The verse says the LOVE of money — which is the point: it is about greed, not money itself.
Developed by St Augustine (4th–5th century) and Thomas Aquinas (13th century). It is not in the Bible. A war is only just if it meets ALL the conditions.

items: Just cause — e.g. defending against attack.
Proper (legitimate) authority — declared by the government, not a group or individual.
Right intention — to promote good and restore peace, not for revenge or gain.
Last resort — every peaceful option has been tried.
Reasonable chance of success.
Proportionality — the good achieved must outweigh the harm; no more force than needed. Civilians must not be targeted.

blocks.title: Memory hook
blocks.text: The first three are Aquinas's: Cause, Authority, Intention. Then Last resort, Success, Proportion.
A holy war is fought for a religious cause, authorised by a religious leader.

rows: The Old Testament describes battles for the Promised Land. In the Crusades (11th–13th centuries) Christians fought Muslims for Jerusalem, believing God was on their side. Holy war is unpopular with Christians today; they follow Jesus: "all who draw the sword will die by the sword" (Matthew 26:52).

Greater jihad is the inner struggle to live as a good Muslim — the more important one. Lesser jihad is the outward struggle to defend Islam, which can mean holy war. It must be defensive, a last resort, declared by a religious leader, and aim to restore peace. It must NOT force anyone to convert, harm women, children or civilians, or destroy homes, places of worship, crops or trees. "Fight in God's cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits" (Qur'an 2:190).

blocks.text: A pacifist believes war and violence can never be justified, even in self-defence.

rows: Many Christian pacifists follow Jesus: "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9). The Quakers are a pacifist denomination; in both world wars they ran the Friends' Ambulance Unit. Conscientious objectors refused to fight but often served as medics or cooks.

Islam promotes peace but is not a pacifist religion, because lesser jihad can be a duty: "Fighting has been ordained for you, though it is hard for you" (Qur'an 2:216). But if the enemy offers peace, Muslims must accept it (Qur'an 8:61).

keyTerms.definition: An absence of conflict, bringing happiness and harmony.
Bringing about what is right and fair.
Letting go of blame against someone who has done wrong.
Restoring friendly relations after conflict.
A public expression of disapproval, often by a group.
The unlawful use of violence, usually against civilians, to achieve a political goal.
Deliberately harming someone in response to them harming you.
A war that meets internationally accepted criteria for fairness.
Fighting for a religious cause, authorised by a religious leader.
The inner struggle to live as a good Muslim.
The outward struggle to defend Islam, including holy war under strict conditions.
The belief that war and violence can never be justified.

examTips: "Religious believers should never fight in a war": FOR — Jesus, Quakers, "blessed are the peacemakers". AGAINST — just war theory, lesser jihad, self-defence in WW2.

Argue FOR the statement with reasons and a teaching. Argue AGAINST with reasons and a teaching. Then a conclusion that weighs them up and says which side is stronger and why. "I agree" on its own is not a conclusion.
commonMistakes: Calling greater jihad "holy war". Holy war is lesser jihad.
Saying Islam is a pacifist religion. It values peace but allows defensive war.

title: Theme B: Religion and belief in 21st-century conflict
summary: Whether religion causes war today, nuclear weapons and deterrence, other weapons of mass destruction, religious peacemakers, and how religious organisations help the victims of war.

sections.title: Religion as a cause of war

blocks.text: Religion can be a cause — or an excuse — for conflict: extremist groups such as Islamic State claim religious reasons for violence. But most conflicts are mainly about land, power, resources or national identity, with religion as a label. Christianity and Islam both teach peace, and most believers reject violence done in their name.

Weapons of mass destruction kill huge numbers and cannot tell soldiers from civilians: nuclear, chemical (poison gas) and biological (spreading disease). Nuclear deterrence is holding nuclear weapons so that no one dares attack you. The UK's deterrent is Trident. Supporters point to no world war since 1945.

rows: "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13) and the sanctity of life go against using them. They fail proportionality — "eye for eye" was about a proportionate response, not "many eyes for an eye". Some Christians accept keeping them as a deterrent but never using them. Pope Francis said in 2019 that even possessing them is immoral.

Life is sacred. War must stay within limits: "do not overstep the limits" (Qur'an 2:190). WMDs kill civilians and destroy the environment, so breach the rules of lesser jihad. "Do not contribute to your destruction with your own hands" (Qur'an 2:195). Some argue deterrence is acceptable for defence.

items: Archbishop Desmond Tutu (Christian) led South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission after apartheid.
Imam Muhammad Ashafa and Pastor James Wuye, former enemies in Nigeria, set up the Interfaith Mediation Centre together.
The Community of the Cross of Nails (Coventry Cathedral) runs reconciliation projects in conflict zones.
Ways believers work for peace: prayer, protest, campaigning, interfaith dialogue, and supporting peace charities.

rows: Works to end poverty worldwide, including helping refugees from war. Slogan: "We believe in life before death". Motivated by "Love your neighbour as yourself" and the Parable of the Good Samaritan.

UK charity founded in 1984. Gives emergency aid in disasters and war, and long-term help to rebuild communities. Helps anyone regardless of race, politics, gender or belief. "Whoever saves a life, it is as if he saved the lives of all mankind" (Qur'an 5:32).

keyTerms.definition: Weapons that can kill large numbers of people and cause great damage — nuclear, chemical, biological.
Holding nuclear weapons to stop others attacking.
Someone who works to establish peace.
Someone forced to leave their country because of war or persecution.

examTips: Learn ONE organisation in detail — name, what it does, and the teaching behind it. That is a full 5-marker.
